intro:
By the end of this track you can predict what Redis does with a command before you send it: which thread runs it, how much memory the key costs, when it expires or gets evicted, whether a sequence of commands is atomic, what survives a crash, and which node of a cluster holds it. You will have built the payment-service patterns that depend on those answers, in Java and in Kotlin: a cache that survives a stampede, a WATCH-based transfer and a Lua ledger, a rate limiter, an idempotency store, a lock with fencing tokens, and a Streams worker that recovers a crashed consumer's messages.

You need to read Java or Kotlin and to have used Redis through a client library; nothing about its internals. Lesson 1 builds the model the rest of the track uses: one thread runs every command to completion. Each later lesson adds to it, and the operating systems track's lessons on copy-on-write, malloc and the page cache come back in lessons 10 and 11, with a one-line reminder each time.

The labs live in `labs/redis`, one package per lesson (`sfz.redis.l01` to `sfz.redis.l11`). Each lab is a failing test suite: run `./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.redis.lNN.*'` from the `labs` folder and make it pass; `src/solution` holds reference answers, which `./gradlew :redis:solutionTest` checks. Model labs (an event loop, sampled LRU, a HyperLogLog, a replication backlog, a cluster router) need only a JDK. The others start a pinned `redis:8.10.3` container through Testcontainers, so Docker must be running. Try-its use `env/redis.yml` (one server, plus a tiny `small` one for eviction), `env/redis-ha.yml` (a primary, a replica and three Sentinels) and `env/redis-cluster.yml` (three cluster nodes). Everything was tested with Redis 8.10.3, Jedis 8.0.2, Lettuce 7.9.0, Testcontainers 2.0.5 and JDK 25; lessons name the Redis version of every command newer than 7.2.
cheatsheet:
### The model

One thread runs every command to completion, one after another. So **every single command is atomic**, and **one slow command stalls every client**. Background threads, forked children and I/O threads (`io-threads`, off by default) never run commands.

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Is one command atomic? | Yes, always. A sequence of commands is not. |
| What makes Redis slow for everyone? | One O(N) command (`KEYS`, `HGETALL` on a big hash, `DEL` of a big key, a long script), a fork, a starved VM. |
| Round trip vs command | A `GET` costs about half a microsecond of server time and a few hundred microseconds of network. Batch round trips. |

### Types (lessons 2 and 3)

| Need | Type | Watch out |
|---|---|---|
| A value, a counter | string: `SET`, `INCR` | a plain `SET` drops the TTL; use `KEEPTTL` |
| An object's fields | hash: `HSET`, `HINCRBY` | listpack up to 512 fields of 64 bytes, then a hash table |
| A ranking | sorted set: `ZADD`, `ZRANGE ... REV` | ties sort by member; ranks start at 0; listpack up to 128 |
| Membership | set | `SMEMBERS` on a big set is O(N); use `SSCAN` |
| Daily active cards | bitmap: `SETBIT`, `BITCOUNT` | needs a dense integer id per card |
| Distinct count | HyperLogLog: `PFADD`, `PFCOUNT` | 12 KB, 0.81% standard error, can't list members |
| Nearby terminals | geo (a sorted set) | distances assume a sphere |
| A work queue or event log | stream | trim with `MAXLEN ~` or `MINID ~` |

### Expiry versus eviction (lesson 4)

| | Expiry | Eviction |
|---|---|---|
| Removes | keys whose TTL deadline passed | keys Redis picks when `used_memory` reaches `maxmemory` |
| When | lazily on access, plus a sampling cycle 10 times a second | before a write that needs room |
| You control it with | `EXPIRE`, `SET ... EX`, `PERSIST` | `maxmemory`, `maxmemory-policy` |
| Default | no TTL | `maxmemory 0` (no limit), `noeviction` (writes fail when full) |

Data (idempotency keys, rate limits, locks): `noeviction`, a TTL on every key, an alert near `maxmemory`. Cache: `allkeys-lru`. Separate instances. `volatile-*` policies act like `noeviction` when no key has a TTL.

### Caching (lesson 5)

Cache-aside: `GET`; on a miss read the database and `SET ... EX`. On a write: commit, then `DEL` the key (never `SET` it). Jitter TTLs (3,600 s plus or minus 10%), cache "not found" briefly, and collapse a hot key's misses with single-flight in the JVM or a `SET NX PX` lock across pods.

### Making a sequence safe (lessons 6 to 8)

| Tool | Atomic? | Can branch on a read? | Saves round trips? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MULTI` / `EXEC` | yes, never rolls back | no | yes |
| `WATCH` + `MULTI` | yes, aborts if a watched key changed; retry | yes, in the client | no |
| Lua script / function | yes, runs inside the event loop | yes | yes |
| Pipelining | **no** | no | yes |
| `SET ... IFEQ` (8.4), `INCREX` (8.8) | yes, one command | one condition | yes |

Patterns built on them:

- Rate limit: count and expire in one step (a script, or `INCREX ... EX 60 ENX` on 8.8); a sliding window is a sorted set trimmed, counted and added to by one script.
- Idempotency key: `SET idem:<key> <pending> NX GET PX 30000` before the work, where the pending value carries the body's hash and an owner token; after it, the stored response as DONE for 24 hours (`SET ... IFEQ <my pending>` on 8.4).
- Lock: `SET lock:<r> <token> NX PX <ttl>`; release with compare-and-delete (a script, or `DELEX key IFEQ token` on 8.4). A lease can expire under a paused holder, so for correctness the resource must check a **fencing token**.

### Messaging (lesson 9)

| | Pub/sub | Stream with a consumer group |
|---|---|---|
| Stores messages | no | yes, until trimmed |
| Delivery | at most once, to whoever is subscribed now | at least once: the PEL keeps each entry until `XACK` |
| A consumer dies | its messages are gone | `XAUTOCLAIM` (or `XREADGROUP ... CLAIM`, 8.4) hands them to another |
| Use for | signals a receiver can miss: cache invalidation, live status | work: settlements, webhooks, retries |

### Durability and failover (lesson 10)

| | Process killed (kill -9, OOM) | Machine dies (power, kernel panic) | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| No persistence | everything | everything | none |
| RDB, default save points | writes since the last snapshot: minutes | the same | a fork plus copy-on-write pages per snapshot |
| AOF `everysec` (default) | nothing | about the last second | one background fsync a second |
| AOF `always` | nothing | nothing | an fsync per event-loop pass: far fewer writes a second |

Replication is asynchronous: a replica follows the stream with an offset, and after a break resyncs from the backlog (`repl-backlog-size`, 1 MB) or with a full snapshot. `WAIT n ms` counts replicas that have this connection's writes; it undoes nothing. `WAITAOF` (7.2) waits for fsync.

| | Sentinel | Cluster |
|---|---|---|
| Data | one primary holds everything | split over primaries by hash slot |
| Failover | 3 or more Sentinels: a quorum agrees, a majority acts | the other primaries vote for a replica |
| Clients | ask a Sentinel for the primary | load the slot table, follow `MOVED` and `ASK` |
| Multi-key commands | anything | only keys in one slot: use hash tags |

### Cluster (lesson 11)

`slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384`; only the part inside the first `{...}` is hashed when there is one. `MOVED <slot> <addr>`: update your table. `ASK <slot> <addr>`: send this one command there after `ASKING`. `CROSSSLOT`: a multi-key command, transaction or script spans slots. Tag by the smallest unit that must change atomically (`{payment:p-981}`), never by tenant.

### When Redis is slow (lesson 11)

| Check | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| `SLOWLOG GET 10` | commands that ran over 10 ms on the command thread |
| `LATENCY LATEST`, `LATENCY DOCTOR` | forks, fsyncs, expiry cycles (set `latency-monitor-threshold` first) |
| `INFO commandstats` | calls and microseconds per command |
| `INFO persistence`, `INFO stats` | `latest_fork_usec`, `rdb_last_cow_size`, `evicted_keys`, `expired_keys` |
| `INFO memory` | `used_memory`, `used_memory_rss`, `mem_fragmentation_ratio` |
| `redis-cli --bigkeys`, `--memkeys`, `HOTKEYS` (8.6) | big keys and hot keys |
| `redis-cli --intrinsic-latency 100` | stalls of the machine itself |

Never `KEYS` in production: `SCAN` with `MATCH` and `COUNT`. `UNLINK`, not `DEL`, for big keys.

### Java and Kotlin

| | Jedis 8 | Lettuce 7.9 |
|---|---|---|
| Entry point | `RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort(h, p).build()` | `RedisClient.create("redis://h:p")`, then `connect()` |
| Connections | a pool: one connection per call | one multiplexed connection |
| Style | blocking calls | sync, async, reactive, Kotlin coroutines (`coroutines()`) |
| Pipelines and WAIT | `redis.pipelined()`: one connection for the batch | every call on the shared connection |
| Cluster | `RedisClusterClient` | `io.lettuce.core.cluster.RedisClusterClient` |
| Sentinel | `RedisSentinelClient` | `RedisURI.Builder.sentinel(...)` |

### Commands by version

| Since | Commands |
|---|---|
| 7.0 | functions (`FUNCTION LOAD`, `FCALL`), multi-part AOF, `EXPIRE ... NX/XX/GT/LT`, sharded pub/sub |
| 7.2 | `WAITAOF` |
| 7.4 | `HEXPIRE` and the other hash-field TTLs |
| 8.4 | `SET ... IFEQ`, `DELEX`, `XREADGROUP ... CLAIM`, `CLUSTER MIGRATION` |
| 8.6 | `XADD ... IDMP`, LRM eviction, `HOTKEYS` |
| 8.8 | `INCREX`, `XNACK` |
| 8.10 | `BACKUP` |

Valkey (BSD, forked from Redis 7.2.4 in 2024) runs everything up to 7.2; check the newer commands before relying on them there.
recap: One thread runs every command to completion: each command is atomic without locks, and one O(N) command, fork or starved VM delays every client.
Choose a type by the operation you need. Small collections are compact listpacks until a size threshold; a key that grows big turns its O(N) commands into outages.

Expiry removes keys whose deadline passed, lazily and by sampling; eviction removes keys Redis chooses when `maxmemory` is full. Data gets `noeviction` and TTLs, a cache `allkeys-lru`, in separate instances.
Cache-aside reads the cache first and deletes the key after a database commit; jittered TTLs and single-flight keep expiries from turning into stampedes.
A sequence of commands is safe only as one atomic step: MULTI/EXEC (no branching, no rollback), WATCH with a retry, or a Lua script. Pipelining only saves round trips.
Rate limits, idempotency keys and locks each check and record in one command or script. A lock is a lease, so correctness needs a fencing token that the resource checks.
Pub/sub delivers at most once to whoever listens now; a stream with a consumer group delivers at least once and lets another worker claim a crashed one's entries, so handlers must be idempotent.
RDB snapshots lose minutes, the AOF with everysec about a second on a machine crash and nothing on a process crash. Replication is asynchronous: WAIT counts copies, Sentinel promotes a replica.
Redis Cluster splits keys into 16,384 slots. Clients route by slot and follow MOVED and ASK; multi-key commands need one slot, which hash tags provide.
When Redis is slow, look for one slow command first (SLOWLOG, LATENCY, commandstats), then forks, big and hot keys, and the machine. SCAN, never KEYS; UNLINK for big keys.

quiz.q: A rate limiter runs `INCR rl:card:7`, and if the result is 1, `EXPIRE rl:card:7 60`. A pod is killed between the two calls. What happens, and what fixes it?
options: Nothing: Redis runs both commands as one step because they come from the same client
The counter has no TTL and never resets, so the card stays blocked; do both in one Lua script, or `INCREX ... EX 60 ENX` on Redis 8.8
Redis notices the missing EXPIRE and sets a default TTL
The INCR is rolled back when the connection drops
quiz.why: Each command is atomic because one thread runs it to the end (lesson 1), but two commands are two steps, and a crash can fall between them (lesson 7). Nothing in Redis ties the INCR to the EXPIRE that should follow, and there is no rollback. A script runs the count and the deadline as one command, and Redis 8.8's INCREX does it natively.

quiz.q: A per-merchant sorted set grows from 120 to 140 members, and `MEMORY USAGE` on it jumps about tenfold. Why?
options: Past 128 members (`zset-max-listpack-entries`) Redis converts the compact listpack into a skip list plus a hash table, and never converts back
The members got longer
The sorted set was copied for a snapshot
Scores became doubles
quiz.why: Small sorted sets live in a listpack, one compact block of memory. At 129 members (or a member over 64 bytes) Redis converts the key to a skip list and a hash table, with pointers and headers for every member: about 1 KB became 11 KB on the lab server (lesson 2). Scores are always doubles, and snapshots don't change a key's encoding.

quiz.q: You must count distinct cards per merchant per day, about 10 million cards in all, within about 1%, in as little memory as possible. Which structure?
options: A set of card ids per merchant per day
A sorted set scored by time
A HyperLogLog per merchant per day: at most 12 KB each, 0.81% standard error
A hash of card id to count
quiz.why: A HyperLogLog estimates distinct counts in at most 12 KB whatever the count, with a 0.81% standard error, and PFMERGE gives the union across days (lesson 3). A set or hash stores every id, hundreds of megabytes at this scale. The price: it can't list or remove members.

quiz.q: An idempotency store runs with `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru`. Under memory pressure a 23-hour-old key disappears although its TTL was 24 hours, and a retried payment is charged twice. What removed it?
options: Expiry: Redis expires keys early when memory is tight
A replica deleted it
The active expiry cycle sampled it by mistake
Eviction: allkeys-lru picked the key idle longest, whatever its TTL
quiz.why: Expiry only removes keys whose deadline has passed, and never early. Eviction removes keys Redis chooses when `used_memory` reaches `maxmemory`, and under allkeys-lru the oldest unread key goes first: a 23-hour-old idempotency key is the perfect candidate (lesson 4). Data like this belongs on an instance with `noeviction`, a `maxmemory` and an alert.

quiz.q: A merchant's row in Oracle has just been updated. What should the service do with the merchant's cached copy in Redis?
options: `SET` the new value into the cache before the database commit
`SET` the new value into the cache after the commit
Commit, then `DEL` the cache key, and let the next read load it
Nothing: the TTL will fix it
quiz.why: Two writers that each SET the cache can finish in the opposite order from their commits and leave the older value cached until the TTL ends (lesson 5). Deleting after the commit only ever removes data; the next reader loads what the database now says. The TTL still caps any race that remains, which is why every cache entry has one.

quiz.q: Debit a prepaid card only if its balance covers the amount, atomically and in one round trip. Which tool fits?
options: MULTI with GET, a check, then DECRBY
A pipeline of GET and DECRBY
A Lua script that reads the balance, checks it and decrements it
Two commands with WATCH but no retry
quiz.why: MULTI queues commands and can't branch on a value read inside it, and it never rolls back (lesson 6). A pipeline only batches round trips; other clients' commands can run between its commands. WATCH works, but needs a retry loop and at least two round trips. A script runs the read, the test and the write as one command on the event loop.

quiz.q: A payout worker holds a Redis lock with a 30-second lease, then stalls in a 40-second GC pause. Another worker takes the lock and writes. The first resumes and writes too. What stops the stale write?
options: Releasing the lock with compare-and-delete
A longer lease
Redlock across five masters
A fencing token from the lock that the payout store checks, refusing any token lower than the highest it has seen
quiz.why: Compare-and-delete stops the first worker from deleting the second's lock, but it doesn't stop its write. A longer lease or Redlock only moves the window; no lease can stop a holder that doesn't know it lost the lock (lesson 8). Only the resource can refuse the stale holder, and the fencing token is how it tells them apart.

quiz.q: Settlement events must survive a worker restart and each be settled at least once, even when a worker crashes halfway through a batch. Pub/sub or Streams?
options: Pub/sub: it is faster
A stream with a consumer group: entries stay pending until XACK, and XAUTOCLAIM hands a crashed worker's entries to another
Pub/sub with a longer client timeout
A stream read with XREAD and no group
quiz.why: Pub/sub stores nothing: a message published while a subscriber is restarting is gone, at most once (lesson 9). A consumer group records every delivery in its pending entries list until the worker acknowledges it, and another worker can claim entries that sit idle too long. That is at least once, so settlement must be idempotent. Plain XREAD keeps the entries but tracks no deliveries.

quiz.q: The machine running Redis loses power. Which configuration loses fewer acknowledged writes, and roughly how many?
options: RDB with the default save points: nothing, since snapshots are on disk
They lose the same: both write to disk
The AOF with everysec: about the last second. RDB loses everything since the last snapshot, often minutes
The AOF with everysec: nothing, since every write is logged before the reply
quiz.why: A snapshot holds the data as of its fork; with save points that is up to minutes old (lesson 10). The AOF passes every write to the kernel before replying, which protects against a process crash, but a power cut also empties the page cache, so writes not yet fsynced are lost: about one second under everysec. Only `always` loses nothing, at a large cost in throughput.

quiz.q: The idempotency store will need 300 GB and 1 million commands a second, far more than one server. Sentinel or Cluster?
options: Cluster: it splits the keys over many primaries by hash slot, each with its own replica and failover
Sentinel: it adds servers when memory runs low
Sentinel with more replicas, reading from all of them
Either: they are two names for the same thing
quiz.why: Sentinel watches one primary that holds every key and promotes a replica when it fails; replicas copy everything, so they split neither the memory nor the writes (lessons 10 and 11). Cluster gives each primary a share of the 16,384 slots and fails each one over separately. The price is that multi-key commands, transactions and scripts need their keys in one slot.
